Cultivar and Air Circulation in Veggie

Red romaine lettuce Lactuca sativa cv. ‘Outredgeous’ was grown in Veggie rooting pillows as described by Massa et al. (2017a).

text:
ISS Red Romaine Lettuce — Source Excerpts for RAG
Fan Failure After a Power Cycle and Early Excess Moisture

Poor air circulation can cause persistent droplets of moisture on the surface of a leaf due to transpiration producing a micro environment favorable for microbial proliferation. In the case of the three Veggie plantings on the ISS, environmental data collected by HOBO data recorders (Supplementary Table S1) showed that temperature and humidity were slightly higher inside the Veggie chamber during the first 22 days of VEG-03A growth than the other two Veggie tests. Additionally, germinating seedlings in the VEG-03A test had excess moisture in the early period of growth, likely due to a fan malfunction, when compared to the VEG-01A and VEG-01B plants. It was during this experiment that our team identified a consistent anomaly with the Veggie hardware – specifically that when power is cycled to the hardware, upon restarting the fan will read “low” but it will actually be off. This problem also led to issues of excess moisture in an earlier Zinnia test but a repetition of this with lettuce confirmed the anomaly.

Logged data from VEG-03A were not collected for the duration of the 64 days experiment so it is speculative to conclude any correlation between microbial counts and Veggie chamber conditions.

Leaf tissue from flight and ground experiments were analyzed for changes in elemental composition (Table 7). There was no significant differences between ground and flight samples within each experiment, however when comparing among all three experiments, Fe and K content were significantly lower in VEG-03A samples compared to VEG-01A and VEG-01B (Fe, P ≤ 0.001; K, P ≤ 0.0001). On the other hand, Na content was found to be significantly higher in VEG-01B compared to VEG-01A or VEG-03A (P ≤ 0.0001). Phosphate (P) measured among all three experiments showed that VEG-01B had higher P contents than VEG-01A and VEG-03A (P ≤ 0.05). Similarly, sulfate measured as S and Zn contents were statistically higher in VEG-01B compared to either VEG-01A or VEG-03A (S, P ≤ 0.05; Zn, P ≤ 0.0001). No significant differences were observed in either Ca, Mg, or Mn content.

text:
Growing red-leaf lettuce under reduced atmospheric pressure
Rockwool substrate, recirculating hydroponics and plant spacing

All plants were grown in 140 × 40 cm stainless steel troughs in a rockwool substrate (Grodan™, Coppell, TX) using a recirculating nutrient film technique delivery system. A 5 cm wide x 3 cm deep “channel” was cut into the bottom of the rockwool to promote nutrient solution flow. The rockwool was rinsed with DI water prior to use to remove particulate material from the substrate.

‘Outredgeous’ was spaced in the rockwool substrate at 15 cm centers within and between troughs, and ‘Flandria’ was spaced at 12 cm centers within and between troughs. Stainless steel plates were placed over the rockwool between plants to minimize algae growth and reduce evaporation rates (Fig. 1B).

text:
Growing red-leaf lettuce under reduced atmospheric pressure
Light, temperature and gas partial pressures

Lighting was provided from six 1000 W metal halide (MH) (P.L. Light Systems, Beamsville, ON, Canada) lamps, which were cycled to provide a 16 h light/08-h dark photoperiod at 300 μmol m⁻² s⁻¹ PPF (17.3 mol m⁻² d⁻¹). Air temperatures were maintained at a constant 22 °C; Vapor Pressure Deficit (VPD) was maintained at a constant 0.9 kPa (~ 62% RH) for the duration of the experiment (Table 1).

CO₂ was maintained at 1200 μ mol⁻¹ (0.12 kPa) partial pressure, and O₂ was maintained at ~21 kPa partial pressure in all chambers.

CO₂ concentration was not controlled during the dark cycle.

The abstract lists a daily light integral of 17.2 mol m⁻² d⁻¹, and §2.1 lists 17.3 mol m⁻² d⁻¹. Oxygen accounted for about 63.5% of total pressure in the nominal 33 kPa treatment. The authors report that the effect of that O₂ percentage is unknown. Total pressure varied across treatments while O₂ partial pressure was held near 21 kPa. The paper did not test a pressure drop with the O₂ fraction kept at 21%.

text:
Growing red-leaf lettuce under reduced atmospheric pressure
Nutrient solution pH, EC and reservoir replenishment

Solution was automatically controlled to near 5.8 pH with additions of dilute nitric acid (0.4 M HNO₃). Water depletion from the nutrient reservoirs due to evapotranspiration was monitored and condensate added back to the reservoir.

Both cultivars received a modified half-strength Hoagland’s nutrient solution in this recirculating rockwool NFT system. Electrical conductivity (EC) was monitored and maintained near 1200 μS cm⁻¹ (1.2 dS m⁻¹) by adding a complete stock solution. These values describe the experimental hydroponic setup.

Visual appearance and chlorophyll under low pressure

Even though the plants appeared smaller under reduced atmospheric pressure, they appeared healthy and showed no visual signs of tissue damage. In addition, the purple/red pigmentation (anthocyanins) of ‘Outredgeous’ appeared more intense under hypobaric than under ambient pressure (Fig. 2).

text:
LED light recipes for Outredgeous red romaine lettuce
Baseline conditions in the ground growth chamber

NASA Kennedy Space Center tested seven fixed LED spectra on red romaine lettuce (*Lactuca sativa* cv. ‘Outredgeous’) in a ground growth chamber for 28 days. The study targeted future Advanced Plant Habitat (APH) experiments aboard the ISS. The chamber was held at 23 ± 0.4 °C, 65 ± 3% relative humidity, and 1,200 ± 60 ppm CO₂. Measured air speed ranged from about 0.5 to 1.0 m/s. The canopy PPFD target was about 180 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ over 400–700 nm, with 18 h of light and 6 h of darkness daily (DLI ≈ 12 mol m⁻² day⁻¹).

text:
LED light recipes for Outredgeous red romaine lettuce
Sowing, germination, sub-irrigation, and thinning

In the ground chamber, four ‘Outredgeous’ seeds were surface-sown per pot on moist Arcillite. Each pot contained 500 mL of medium mixed with 18-6-8 controlled-release NPK fertilizer at 7.5 g per liter of dry medium. The pots sat in sub-irrigation trays containing about 1 cm of deionized water. For the first three days, the researchers used clear covers and misted with deionized water to promote germination. They measured tray water levels and logged the amount added daily. On day 7 they removed one plant per pot, choosing the weakest or an unsuccessfully germinated seedling. They harvested plants for growth measurements at 14, 21, and 28 DAS.

Early growth at 7–14 days after sowing

Under white + green (WG), ‘Outredgeous’ seedlings showed earlier hypocotyl elongation and faster first true-leaf expansion by 7 DAS. At 14 DAS, WG shoot fresh mass was significantly above the white control, while red + blue (RB) was significantly below it. LED light recipes for Outredgeous red romaine lettuce
Late growth and harvest biomass at 21–28 days after sowing

In ‘Outredgeous’ red romaine lettuce, early growth under white + green (WG) slowed after 21 DAS. Under white + red (WR), shoot dry mass rose more rapidly late in the cycle (21–28 DAS). At the 28 DAS harvest, both WG and WR dry mass were statistically comparable to the white control (W). RGB + FR gave the highest shoot fresh mass and dry mass. Of the tested spectra, only RGB + FR (higher) and RB (lower) differed significantly from W in final shoot dry mass. RGB + FR had the greatest mean leaf area, with WFR in the same statistical group for that comparison.

text:
LED light recipes for Outredgeous red romaine lettuce
Leaf pigmentation and nutrient concentrations

At 14 DAS, ‘Outredgeous’ leaves looked darker under WB and RB, both of which supplied at least 40% blue light within the 400–700 nm band. The authors describe the color response visually. At 28 DAS, WB had the highest reported leaf potassium concentration, and RB had the highest measured lutein concentration. Lutein concentrations under WB, WG, and WR were statistically comparable to W. RGB + FR had lower concentrations of the four displayed minerals (Ca, K, Mg, and P), and both WFR and RGB + FR had lower lutein concentrations than W. The nutrient figures report concentration per gram of dry tissue.

text:
LED light recipes for Outredgeous red romaine lettuce
Leaf and petiole responses under far-red recipes

In ‘Outredgeous’ red romaine lettuce, both WFR and RGB + FR produced wider shoots than white at 21 DAS. At 28 DAS, WFR produced the tallest shoots (26.5 cm), with elongated petioles and shoot dry mass statistically comparable to white. RGB + FR produced a large leaf area and the highest dry mass. The far-red fluxes were similar for the two recipes (34 and 36 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹), while their red-to-far-red ratios were 1.7 and 3.1, respectively.

text:
LED light recipes for Outredgeous red romaine lettuce
Proposed light-recipe switches during the crop cycle

The authors suggest testing a switch from white + green (WG) to white + red (WR) or RGB + FR at 21 days after sowing to see whether final ‘Outredgeous’ yield improves. They also propose testing a switch from WB or RB to WR to balance yield and nutrient concentration. The experiment compared fixed, full-cycle light recipes, so the effects of mid-cycle switching remain untested in this study.

Root-Zone pH, Electrical Conductivity, and Yield Decline

Opening Germination Wicks on Day 3 and Thinning Seedlings on Day 7

VEG-01A/B Lighting Settings and Photoperiod

LED lights were set to red and blue on high and green on, with the bellows baseplate positioned 30.5-31.75 cm below the light array to provide approximately 200 µmol·m²·s⁻¹ of photosynthetically active radiation at the surface of the pillows in the center of the Veggie unit at a ratio of 12 red (630 nm): 3 Blue (455 nm): 1 green (530 nm). A photoperiod was set to 16 h light / 8 h dark.

The VEG-01B test was initiated by ISS astronaut Scott Kelly in July, 2015, with the same lighting and photoperiod settings as VEG-01A.

Photos were taken weekly, and photos at 14 days after initiation showed that three of the five plants were stunted and did not appear to be growing. The original non-functional plant pillow A had been saved from VEG-01A, and the quick disconnect water attachment had been swapped after harvest with one that was known to function. Kelly attempted to prime this plant pillow in VEG-01B but again water was unable to enter, indicating failure in a component other than the quick disconnect. text:
VEG-03 J | Growing Red Romaine in ISS Veggie with Seed Film
Seed film material and function

Scientists at NASA’S Kennedy Space Center (KSC) developed a food-safe water-soluble polymer known as seed film into which seeds can be embedded for storage and planting. The reported properties of several polymers were evaluated, and a pullulan formulation was developed, tested, and selected, with the methodology refined to produce a functional approach.

Seed films were created by combining 9 g pullulan (TCI America, Portland, OR), 1 g food-grade glycerol, and 90 g deionized water and stirring the solution overnight to allow the polymer to dissolve completely.

metadata.section: VEG-03 J | Growing Red Romaine in ISS Veggie with Seed Film
metadata.subsection: Seed film material and function
metadata.source_location: Abstract, p. 506; §2.1 Seed film preparation, p. 507

text:
VEG-03 J | Growing Red Romaine in ISS Veggie with Seed Film
Preparing a three-seed film coupon

Individual, sanitized ‘Outredgeous’ seeds were placed on the film surface in groupings of three with 2.54 cm of separation between the edge of each grouping. Following placement, 10 μL aliquots of sterile, deionized water were placed on each seed before allowing the droplets to fully dry, resulting in total encapsulation of the seeds within the seed film. The grouped, encapsulated seeds were then cut into 6.45 cm² (1 in²) coupons, and a small, triangular notch was cut into the bottom edge of each coupon to indicate the planting orientation (Fig. 1).

metadata.section: VEG-03 J | Growing Red Romaine in ISS Veggie with Seed Film
metadata.subsection: Preparing a three-seed film coupon

text:
VEG-03 J | Growing Red Romaine in ISS Veggie with Seed Film
Plant pillow substrate and fertilizer

Twelve pillows (6 for flight, 6 for ground) were prepared following methods as described by Massa et al. [9]. Pillow substrate was a 1:1 mix of 600 μm-1 mm and 1-2 mm porous ceramic (Profile Products LLC Greensgrade and Turface Pro-League, respectively). Fertilizer was added into the substrate in the following amounts: Nutricote 18-6-8 T70 fertilizer: 1.000-1.0049 g per pillow; Nutricote 18-6-8 T180 fertilizer: 1.2500-1.2549 g (Florikan ESA, Sarasota, FL) per pillow for a total rate of 9 g fertilizer per liter substrate.

metadata.section: VEG-03 J | Growing Red Romaine in ISS Veggie with Seed Film
metadata.subsection: Plant pillow substrate and fertilizer

VEG-03 J | Growing Red Romaine in ISS Veggie with Seed Film
Day 0 sowing and initial watering

During planting, wicks were spread open and seed film coupons were inserted with the notch toward the bottom of the pillow allowing the top of the coupon to remain just above the top edge of the pillow gasket. Following coupon placement, wicks were returned to the closed position, and pillows were initiated with 150 mL water from the ISS Potable Water Dispenser.

VEG-03 J | Growing Red Romaine in ISS Veggie with Seed Film
Germination and harvested fresh mass

As seed film was a new technology, three seeds were inserted into each Veggie pillow, instead of the former seeding rate of two per pillow, to increase chances that each pillow would ultimately have at least one successfully germinated and established plant. Germination on the ISS was highly successful (94%) with only one out of 18 seeds failing to germinate. Ground germination was comparatively lower (67%), potentially due to water behavior issues; future testing is anticipated to clarify this. All pillows in both flight (total harvested plants [n2] = 6) and ground (n2 = 6) had successful plant growth for the entire test (Fig. 2), which had been a challenge in the past.

text:
VEG-03 J | Growing Red Romaine in ISS Veggie with Seed Film
Pathogen screening and yeast and mold counts at harvest

Despite having a higher mean heterotrophic plate count value than other Veggie technology demonstrations, the VEG-03 J samples returned negative results on all performed pathogen-specific screening tests. These results were corroborated by the absence of pathogenic organisms in the 16S rRNA data.

The samples also returned countable IMA plates to provide yeast and mold data for flight and ground. None of the sample sets differed significantly from each other between technology demonstrations or between flight and ground experiments (p > 0.05). All the ground samples, including those collected in VEG-03 J, were found to have a mean culturable fungal load lower than the current NASA safety standards for non-thermostabilized foods: 1 × 10³ Colony Forming Units (CFU) g⁻¹ [20]. The only flight samples below this threshold value were from VEG-01 A (μ = 5.6 × 10² CFU g⁻¹). At present, these are the closest approximate standards for the evaluation of food safety of fresh grown produce in a flight scenario. Other standards for the evaluation of food safety of these commodities in situ are in development.
